rv.q: The plays may not always be your cup of tea — filled with spare language, ambiguity, unreliability and disintegration — but there can be no complaints about the service.
McKellen and Stewart make a riveting duo as the principal performers destined – or doomed – for eternity to play out routines of existential unease and encroaching mortality.

Both actors, neither one immune to the lure of excess showmanship, are terrific -- stylish, disciplined, strikingly different -- in Sean Mathias' repertory stagings of Beckett's familiar 1953 masterwork, "Waiting for Godot," and Pinter's more rare, chilling and opaque "No Man's Land."
These shows are an irresistible celebration of two actors’ love affairs with their scripts.
Who wouldn’t want the privilege of watching him in action?
I only wish I had found a bit more enjoyment in this production.
The ease of their companionship is almost infectious, elevating these productions to the sublime.

Director Sean Mathias and his talented quartet of actors (they are billed above the title alphabetically as Billy Crudup, Shuler Hensley, Ian McKellen and Patrick Stewart) do lovely service to both of them.
Both Land and Godot, in fact, prove that the most challenging and unsettling material can make for accessible, even buoyant, entertainment.
Stewart and McKellen traverse the full range of humanity on stage, with moments of hope, fear and despair.
More familiar but a bit less successful, Mathias’ “Godot” needs a shot of dread.

Although not as dramatically potent as Pinter's similarly plotted "The Caretaker," the play, like "Godot," gives two commanding performers an opportunity to provide a master class in acting. They're a treat.

cn.t: McKellen and Stewart bring infectious joy and masterful comic timing to Pinter's enigmatic classic, turning existential limbo into compelling entertainment despite the play's inherent obscurity.

vs.sum: A beautifully restored theater with a stunning Tiffany-inspired interior. The 2021 renovation transformed restroom facilities from among Broadway's worst to a model for the industry, with modern bathrooms on every public level.

acc.note: Elevator to Mezzanine, Balcony, and lower level restrooms. 7 wheelchair spaces across all levels.
